title: XML-RPC Abuse & Attacks
description: Stop xmlrpc.php abuse — pingback DDoS, brute force amplification, and unnecessary exposure on sites that do not need XML-RPC.

steps.title: Confirm XML-RPC Is the Attack Vector
steps.instructions: Check server logs for high traffic to /xmlrpc.php. Look for system.multicall brute force attempts or pingback floods in access logs.

steps.title: Check if XML-RPC Is Required
steps.instructions: Jetpack, some mobile apps, and remote publishing tools need XML-RPC. Confirm with client before disabling. WooCommerce and most sites do not need it.

steps.title: Disable XML-RPC via Plugin or Filter
steps.instructions: Use Disable XML-RPC plugin or add remove_action for xmlrpc if not needed. Safer than deleting the file — WordPress may restore it on update.

steps.title: Block xmlrpc.php at Server Level
steps.instructions: Add Apache/nginx deny rule for xmlrpc.php if plugin approach is insufficient. More efficient — blocked before PHP loads.

steps.title: Disable Pingbacks Site-Wide
steps.instructions: Uncheck 'Attempt to notify any blogs linked from the post' under Settings → Writing. Pingbacks are a common DDoS amplification vector.

steps.title: Restrict XML-RPC in Security Plugin
steps.instructions: Wordfence and similar plugins can block xmlrpc.php or allow only authenticated requests. Configure instead of full disable if Jetpack is required.

steps.title: Verify Attack Stopped and Site Functions
steps.instructions: Confirm xmlrpc.php traffic drops in logs. Test Jetpack/mobile app if applicable. Monitor for 48 hours.
